messages.subject: [R-meta] Question Re: Rma.mv Model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks as always!

I wanted to confirm that I understood your instructions above re:
converting multiple correlation types into Fisher's z.  I have a dataframe
with adjusted beta, partial r, rho, beta, and unstandardized b.  Is this
delta correction correct? Note: r_oriented is the effect size and N_Effect
is the sample size --

meta_df_other <- meta_df %>% subset(Reported_Stat_Type != r (Pearson)")
meta_df_other <- escalc(measure = "COR", ri=r_oriented, ni=N_Effect, data =
meta_df_other)
meta_df_other <- conv.delta(yi, vi, data=meta_df_other, transf=transf.rtoz,
replace=TRUE)

On Fri, Sep 25, 2026 at 3:11?AM Viechtbauer, Wolfgang (NP) <
wolfgang.viechtbauer at maastrichtuniversity.nl> wrote:

> EXTERNAL EMAIL - This email was sent by a person from outside your
> organization. Exercise caution when clicking links, opening attachments or
> taking further action, before validating its authenticity.
> With respect to sensitivity analyses:
>
> Many sensitivity analyses involve the typical kinds of choices one has to
> make when conducting a meta-analysis (or really any kind of analysis).
> Gelman and Loken used the metaphor of "the garden of forking paths" to
> describe this idea (not in the context of meta-analysis but more broadly):
>
> Gelman, A., & Loken, E. (2014). The statistical crisis in science.
> American Scientist, 102(6), 460.
> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://doi.org/10.1511/2014.111.460___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6NTI0ZDphYzJjOWMwNDdmYThkZDNkYWFkODY3OThlYzY2Y2E2YmNhZjRlOGQ5ODYwOTM1M2U1MDZlM2M3OTE5N2RhNDhjOnA6VDpG
>
> Simmons and colleagues call this "researcher degrees of freedom":
>
> Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D., & Simonsohn, U. (2011). False-positive
> psychology: Undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis allows
> presenting anything as significant. Psychological Science, 22(11),
> 1359-1366.
> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797611417632___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6ODAxZTo0MmU2MDE5NzhkZGUzYTQxOWQ1YTY1YWIyNjE3ZmQ5NzAyYzFhMjZlNzVlZmQxMTU1OTYxNGEzNzIzMDVhZmFkOnA6VDpG
>
> Of course, none of this is new. The idea that one has to make many
> decisions, judgments, and choices in collecting and analyzing a set of data
> is completely apparent to anybody who has ever been in this situation. In
> the meta-analytic context, this was discussed already early on; for example:
>
> Light, R. J. (1980). Synthesis methods: Some judgment calls that must be
> made. Evaluation in Education, 4, 13-17.
> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://doi.org/10.1016/0191-765X(80)90002-6___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6ODNmNjpjMzI4ZWMyODU4NDAwYTc3Yzk5MzgxNzJlZDU4NDUyMGZhMmVlZjhjMTJlYTc5NjI2ZTcwMmQyNTUwNDE3ZTBkOnA6VDpG
>
> Wanous, J. P., Sullivan, S. E., & Malinak, J. (1989). The role of judgment
> calls in meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 74(2), 259-264.
> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.74.2.259___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6YmIzNjo3OTAyZDMyZThmZGZjNzQ5NTdhNGIzNDA5OGU4Y2I0MjlmNzljZjEyY2ZlYjNmZjhlOWUwYmE4NWI5ZjEzNjcwOnA6VDpG
>
> And more related to the choices around the statistical methods:
>
> Mengersen, K. L., Tweedie, R. L., & Biggerstaff, B. (1995). The impact of
> method choice on meta-analysis. Australian Journal of Statistics, 37(1),
> 19-44.
> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-842X.1995.tb00869.x___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6OGZiMDowODc5ZmJhZDUwYjc4NWQyZTEwMDYzYTFjYjI5MWM0MDY1MTdmZTcyZTMzMTg3NTk5YWE1MDA3MzQ2Y2JmYzI0OnA6VDpG
>
> Describing all these kinds of choices and decision points would take too
> long and some of this is specific to a particular project. But typical
> choices and judgment calls include:
>
> - eligibility: which studies, outcomes, time points, and populations to
> include.
> - effect-size definition: which effect measure to use and how to compute
> it; also which effect size to extract when there are multiple reasonable
> options (e.g., adjusted vs unadjusted odds ratio).
> - data handling: dealing with missing information, multiple outcomes,
> multiple groups, and dependent effects.
> - model choice: equal/common-effect vs. random-effects; potentially
> multilevel/multivariate models.
> - estimation: estimator for heterogeneity, inference method,
> confidence/prediction intervals.
> - heterogeneity: how to assess it and which moderators/subgroups to
> examine via meta-regression or subgrouping.
> - study quality: how risk of bias and/or study quality are evaluated and
> how they enter the analysis.
> - Outliers/influential studies: whether and how to identify and handle
> them.
> - Publication bias: which diagnostics and adjustment/sensitivity methods
> to use.
>
> Hence, there isn't a sensitivity() function. Instead, you have to think
> about these choices, their potential impact, and which ones you think need
> to be examined (which is yet another choice - it's INCEPTION all over
> again). You do this by going down the alternative path in the garden to see
> what happens (e.g., what happens when I DO remove the non-randomized
> studies? what happens when I assume a pre-post correlation of 0.7 or 0.1
> instead of 0.4? what happens when I exclude this or that study?).
>
> Best,
> Wolfgang
>

> https://protect.checkpoint.com/v2/r01/___http://project.org___.YzJ1OnN0b255YnJvb2s6YzpnOmNiNzBkYjYyMTAxNDEwMmYxNjJhZDI4N2VkZjMxYzQxOjc6ZDVmMzplODkwNWE2OTNhZmM0NGFhNzBmNjczNmY5NjczMDA0OGVmMGVmZGVmMWUzNWZmYjY3ZDU5MzQzODM3MDU3OTk0OnA6VDpG
> >
> > > Cc: Tori Pe?a <mailto:Tori.Pena at stonybrook.edu>
> > > Subject: [R-meta] Question Re: Rma.mv Model
> > >
> > > Hello everyone -
> > >
> > > I have a couple of questions related to a three-level model we plan to
> > > conduct using *metafor. *For context, we have compiled correlations
> > > indexing relationships between cognition and inflammation in the body.
> We
> > > plan to nest effect sizes (level 1) in sample cohorts (level 2) within
> > > studies (level 3). I wanted to check the following questions:
> > >
> > >    1. The literature has different types of correlations. Is it
> acceptable
> > >    to convert all of these correlations to Fisher's *z *for the models?
> > >    Or, should there way to handle these varying effect size types?
> >
> > You can use the standard r-to-z transformation on all kinds of
> correlation
> > coefficients. However, the sampling variance equation 1/(n-3) only
> applies when
> > converting Pearson product-moment correlations with the r-to-z
> transformation.
> > For other types of correlation coefficients (Spearman, (point-)biserial,
> > tetrachoric, (semi)partial, and so on), it would not be correct to use
> 1/(n-3)
> > as the variance.
> >
> > Using the delta method, one can compute the variance of any r-to-z
> transformed
> > correlation coefficient as long as one has an estimate of the variance
> of the
> > correlation coefficient to begin with. For example, say you have a study
> that
> > dichotomized both variables of interest and reports the results in terms
> of a
> > 2x2 table (how many people scored above/below the cutoff on the first
> variable
> > versus the second variable). Say this is the 2x2 table:
> >
> >        Above  Below
> > Above  15     5
> > Below   8     18
> >
> > Then we can get the tetrachoric correlation with:
> >
> > dat <- escalc(measure="RTET", ai=15, bi=5, ci=8, di=18)
> > dat
> >
> >       yi     vi
> > 1 0.6397 0.0258
> >
> > (this estimates the correlation between the underlying continuous
> variables). I
> > can now r-to-z transform this with:
> >
> > transf.rtoz(dat$yi)
> > [1] 0.757601
> >
> > But
> >
> > 1/((15+5+8+18)-3)
> > [1] 0.02325581
> >
> > is NOT the sampling variance of the transformed tetrachoric correlation.
> Using
> > the delta method, we can compute a correct (i.e., consistent) estimate
> of the
> > sampling variance:
> >
> > conv.delta(yi, vi, data=dat, transf=transf.rtoz,
> > replace=TRUE)
> >
> >       yi     vi
> > 1 0.7576 0.0740
> >
> > Note that the variance (0.0740) is more than 3 times larger than the
> incorrect
> > estimate (0.0233), because we lost information from the dichotomization
> of the
> > two variables and having to reconstruct the correlation from that
> information.
> > You can actually skip the whole conv.delta() thing since escalc() can
> directly
> > do all of this for you:
> >
> > dat <- escalc(measure="ZTET", ai=15, bi=5, ci=8,
> > di=18)
> > dat
> >
> >
> >
> >       yi     vi
> > 1 0.7576 0.0740
> >
> > The same principle applies to other correlation coefficients. Note that
> the r-
> > to-z transformation is only a variance stabilizing transformation for
> Pearson
> > product-moment correlations, not for (most) other types of correlation
> > coefficients. However, using the transformation can still be
> advantageous, since
> > raw correlations are bounded which can result in skewed sampling
> distributions.
> > The r-to-z transformation can then help to normalize the sampling
> distributions.
> >
> > >    2. I could not find information in the *metafor *documentation about
> > >    conducting sensitivity analyses for rma.mv objects. Is this
> possible? If
> > >    so, how?
> >
> > What type of sensitivity analyses are you thinking of?
> >
> > > Thanks in advance,
> > > Tori
>
